deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematics on this page. Folio 163 is a continuous prose passage in German Kurrent script giving lecture-style notes on Seleucid history. It continues the account of Antiochus III from the previous page and leads into Antiochus IV on the next. Content in order:
(1) Rome demanded that Antiochus III withdraw from the Thracian Chersonese; he refused, and the disputes continued for some years.
(2) Hannibal fled to Antiochus and urged him to make war on Rome.
(3) War broke out in 190; Antiochus was defeated, and his lands went to the king of Pergamon.
(4) Roman peace terms: 1. evacuate all of Asia Minor ('Vorderasien'); 2. pay 15000 talents; 3. surrender Hannibal; [4.] give his younger son to Rome as a hostage.
(5) Antiochus III died soon after; 'in 187 he was murdered'.
(6) He was succeeded by his eldest son, Seleucus IV Philopator, dated 187–176.
(7) To raise money Seleucus 'plundered the Temple in Jerusalem'.
(8) He wanted to exchange his brother, still a hostage in Rome, for his own son Demetrius. 'Bruder' is struck through and corrected to 'Sohn' in the right margin. The Romans agreed.
(9) While both were travelling, the minister Heliodorus had Seleucus murdered and in 176 took the royal title, but could not hold it.
There are no derivations, formulas or computations to reconstruct. The page sits in a bundle catalogued 'HB.Lagrange1816', but its content is ancient history. It is plausibly not Gauss's own text: it may be a family member's or student's lecture notes. The hand is a fairly regular student-style Kurrent and does not obviously match Gauss's; attribution unsure.
errors: Numbering slip in the peace terms: the image shows '3,' written twice (before 'Hannibal auszuliefern' and before 'seinen jüngern Sohn'). The fourth condition is mislabelled 3.
The dates for Seleucus IV (187–176) and for Heliodorus's usurpation (176) are about a year off the modern dating. Seleucus IV is usually dated 187–175 BC and was murdered in 175 BC.
'plünderte er den Tempel zu Jerusalem' simplifies the tradition. In 2 Maccabees 3, Heliodorus is sent to seize the temple treasury and the attempt fails.
'187 wurde er ermordet': Antiochus III was killed in 187 BC while plundering a temple of Bel in Elymais. 'Murdered' is a loose but common characterisation.

Treaty details: the treaty of Apamea (188 BC) required withdrawal west of the Taurus, not literally all of Asia Minor. The defeat (Magnesia) is usually dated 190/189 BC. The 15000 talents and the surrender of Hannibal are correct.

results.what: Historical narrative: Antiochus III's war with Rome, the treaty of Apamea, the reign of Seleucus IV, and Heliodorus's usurpation
results.usually_credited_to: Standard ancient sources (Polybius, Livy, Appian, 2 Maccabees) as transmitted in early-19th-century history lectures

deep.surprise_reason: The page contains no mathematics, only routine school or lecture notes on Hellenistic history, possibly not in Gauss's hand. Nothing here bears on the history of mathematics.

checkable.asserts: Length of Seleucus IV's reign as dated on the page (187–176) is 11 years.
Antiochus III died 3 years after the outbreak of the war as dated on the page ('überlebte die Niederlage nicht lange').

transcription_corrections: Line 8: the item number before 'seinen jüngern Sohn' is written '3,' in the manuscript (a duplicated number), not '4'.
Lines 15–16: 'gegen seinen [-Bruder-] Demetrius' — 'Bruder' is struck through, with marginal insertion '+ Sohn' at right; the reading 'seinen Sohn Demetrius' is correct.

Line 17: the words read as 'ermordete[?] der Minister Heliodor ließ[?]' are uncertain in the image. The phrase looks closer to 'ereignete sich, daß der Minister Heliodor' / 'wagte es der Minister'. In any case the sense is 'the minister Heliodorus had Seleucus murdered'.
Right margin: a Roman numeral 'IV' stands beside 'Seleucus' at line 11 (it belongs to 'Seleucus IV'), and a small mark resembling '3' or '5' stands near line 6; folio number '163' at top right.
Line 2: 'flüchtet' as transcribed matches the image (present tense, inconsistent with the surrounding past tense).
